A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same RDIRL research and provide readable text, equations, tables, and figures. All pages were inspected, including v3's Appendix A. v1 ends with references and has no appendix.

before.justification: Section 6 reports original CartPole, MountainCar, and cognitive-radar simulation results, including learning curves and numerical comparisons.

after.justification: Section 6 reports original results on the retained tasks and additional MuJoCo environments. Appendix A.5 adds experiments with online-adapted comparison methods.

M1.justification: The upper-bound objective, regularizer, parameter and covariance recursions, and per-observation policy updates remain unchanged in Algorithm 1. Appendix A.3 expands the algorithm explanation without specifying a new RDIRL component.

E1.justification: v3 retains CartPole, continuous MountainCar, and cognitive radar, and adds HalfCheetah-v4, Hopper, and Walker2d evaluations. These additional MuJoCo control tasks substantially broaden the empirical coverage.

E2.justification: The reported GAN-GCL comparator, attributed to Finn et al. (2016a), is replaced by AIRL, attributed to Fu et al. (2017), in the retained comparisons. v3 also adds SQIL and Adam-optimized UB to Table 1, and online-adapted GAIL, GCL, and AIRL comparisons in Appendix A.5.

E3.justification: v3 reports continuous-control networks with 16 rather than 32 units per hidden layer, MountainCar trajectories of 200 rather than 150 steps, and longer training horizons. It also introduces expert-normalized Walker2d reporting and per-observation update protocols for the online-adapted baselines.

E4.justification: The new UB-with-Adam comparison tests the empirical usefulness of the surrogate loss alongside conventional optimization. Appendix A.5 separately tests whether adapting competing methods to update after each observation closes the performance gap. v1 contains neither corresponding control analysis.

E5.justification: Continuous-control experiments increase from five to twelve Monte Carlo runs. v3 adds numerical uncertainty values to Table 1 and explicitly identifies learning-curve dispersion as standard deviations. This extends existing repeated-run reporting; radar retains five runs and a mean-only Table 2.

E6.justification: Tables 1–2 replace the original scores: for example, RDIRL's MountainCar mean changes from 5110.09 to 4862.09, and its radar mean from 498.25 to 924.78. Revised settings prevent interpreting these as controlled performance changes. Extensive new results include Hopper, where SQIL's mean reward of 257.15 exceeds RDIRL's 220.79.

T1.justification: v3 adds a brief proof of Theorem 5.1 invoking Lemma B.3 of Humpherys et al. The upper-bound mathematics and recursive-update theorem are otherwise retained. The detailed Newton derivation moves from Section 5 to Appendix A.4, with corresponding equation renumbering.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction's twofold contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same central claims: an upper-bound objective enabling recursive optimization, online neural cost-function learning, and favorable convergence against leading IRL methods. The expanded experiments support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v3 adds interpretations concerning UB's usefulness and the advantages of recursive optimization over naive online adaptation. Section 6.1 introduces expert-proximity when discussing Walker2d and describes highest average rewards in most environments, whereas v1 emphasized uniform superiority across its tested tasks.

D1.justification: Appendix A adds grid-search procedures, Adam and MPPI hyperparameters, covariance initialization, network details, runtimes, baseline implementation sources, and a statement that code accompanies the supplementary material. These substantially expand v1's sparse implementation reporting. However, Appendix A.2's general H200 hardware statement conflicts with Section 6.2's retained radar CPU description.

R1.justification: v3 adds references for SQIL, MuJoCo, the imitation implementation repository, and two Ghanem et al. works supporting the optimization discussion. The related-work section and positioning around combining online learning with neural cost representations remain largely unchanged.

P1.justification: v3 moves the lengthy Section 5 derivation into Appendix A.4, adds an explanatory algorithm walkthrough, revises experimental framing, and updates author information and front matter. These are localized organizational and explanatory changes; the abstract, introduction, related work, background, and conclusion largely retain their wording.

P2.justification: v3 changes the document from two-column to predominantly single-column layout, expands Figure 1 from two to four panels, and enlarges Table 1's comparator and task structure. It adds Walker2d and online-adaptation figures plus hyperparameter and online-comparison tables. The radar figure is redrawn and gains an expert reference curve.

improvement.justification: The UB-with-Adam and online-adapted baseline experiments address an important weakness in v1: limited evidence distinguishing the benefits of the loss and recursive update procedure. Additional MuJoCo validation and substantial implementation disclosures strengthen the empirical foundation and reproducibility. v3's blanket superiority wording conflicts with the Hopper ranking, and hardware reporting is inconsistent, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains.
